title: The Child of the Storm: from a priest's house in the Lika to Room 3327
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Smiljan, the birth at midnight
stops.date_confidence: attested. The coordinates are the Nikola Tesla Memorial Center, which occupies the birth house and the Church of St Peter and Paul; the research pool's geography lens pinned this site 7 km away, in empty Lika terrain, and its own afterlife lens gave the position used here.
stops.campa: In the priest's house at Smiljan, in the Military Frontier where Vienna keeps its Serbs armed along the Ottoman border, a fourth child is born to Milutin Tesla, priest of the Orthodox church beside the house, and to Đuka Mandić, who cannot read and who builds looms. The hour is midnight and a storm stands over the Lika. The midwife calls the boy a child of the storm; the mother answers that he is a child of light. No register preserves the exchange. The district tells it that way regardless, and he never corrects it in print.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed birth house and the Church of St Peter and Paul at Smiljan, now the Nikola Tesla Memorial Center

stops.name: Gospić, the parish and the lower gymnasium
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the move; no month reached. The pool placed the Higher Real Gymnasium here, which is wrong on its own terms: Tesla left for Karlovac in 1870 precisely because the higher school was there.
stops.campa: Milutin takes a larger parish and the family moves down to Gospić, the garrison town of the Lika. The boy of six goes to primary school here and afterward to the lower Real Gymnasium, where a teacher's demonstration apparatus holds him longer than the lessons do. The house expects a priest of him, as it made one of his father and officers of his mother's people. He is set to Latin and liturgy, and spends the hours he can steal on arithmetic done in his head faster than the master can set it on the board.
suggested_refs: The Serbian Orthodox parish of Gospić, held by Milutin Tesla from 1862

stops.name: Karlovac, the Higher Real Gymnasium
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1870 to 1873; no month reached, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He is sent north to Karlovac to board with an aunt and finish at the Higher Real Gymnasium, which Gospić does not have. Marsh fever comes with the town and never quite leaves him. He runs the four-year course in three, and the physics master's demonstrations of electricity settle the question the household has been asking since the night he was born: not the priesthood. He does not yet say so aloud. He writes home that he is well, and says nothing about the seminary that is still waiting for him.
suggested_refs: The Higher Real Gymnasium at Karlovac, completed by Tesla in three years

stops.name: Smiljan, nine months of cholera
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and for the nine months in bed; no month reached. Place corrected: Wikipedia is explicit that Tesla returned to Smiljan after graduating and contracted cholera there, not at Karlovac or Gospić as the pool had it. The bedside bargain is his own account and rests on nothing else.
stops.campa: He graduates and comes home to Smiljan, and cholera is waiting in the village. He lies nine months in the room he was born in, close to death more than once, too weak to hold a book upright. In his own account, written forty-six years afterward, his father sits by the bed and promises the engineering school instead of the seminary, and the promise is the medicine. No one else records the bargain. What is recorded is that he rose, and that the following year the family did not send him to the church.
suggested_refs: Tesla's account of the nine-month illness in My Inventions, Chapter II

stops.name: Graz, the scholarship and the card tables
stops.date_confidence: attested for the enrolment in 1875 and the departure without a degree in December 1878; the month of enrolment is not reached and defaults to January.
stops.campa: On a Military Frontier scholarship he enters the Imperial-Royal Technical College at Graz and works like a man serving a sentence, three in the morning until eleven at night, passing nine examinations in a year the professors thought would take two. A letter goes to his father warning that the son will kill himself with study. By the third year the scholarship is gone and the card tables have taken the rest, and in December 1878 he leaves without a degree and tells no one at home. He is twenty-two and has stopped writing letters.
suggested_refs: The Joanneum, Imperial-Royal Technical College at Graz, where Tesla first saw a Gramme dynamo
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla: Inventor of the Electrical Age (2013), via citation

stops.name: Maribor, the draftsman and the deportation
stops.date_confidence: attested: found working at Maribor in January 1879; Milutin Tesla's death 17 April 1879 is attested to the day and is carried in this stop's campa rather than given its own pin.
stops.campa: He surfaces in Maribor as a draftsman at sixty florins a month, playing cards in the street with the town's men, and is arrested for having no residence permit and put under escort on a train to Gospić. His family had been searching for him for a year. On the seventeenth of April his father dies, aged sixty, and the promise made at the sickbed at Smiljan passes to two uncles, who agree to pay for Prague. He teaches a term at the Gospić gymnasium first, in the town where every household knows whose son he is.
suggested_refs: The grave of Milutin Tesla at Gospić, died 17 April 1879
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla: Inventor of the Electrical Age (2013), via citation

stops.name: Prague, the lectures at the Karolinum
stops.date_confidence: attested for January 1880. Coordinates corrected to the Karolinum, the historic seat of Charles-Ferdinand University; the pool's pin sat 0.9 km west near the Klementinum. That he attended as an auditor rather than a matriculated student is Carlson's reading.
stops.campa: With his uncles' money he goes to Prague and attends lectures at the Charles-Ferdinand University, most probably as an auditor rather than a matriculated student, having no Greek and nothing from Graz to show. He sits in on physics and philosophy for a term and takes no degree here either. Of the three universities in his life, not one issues him a paper. Nothing in the Prague lecture rooms bears on the problem of the commutator. His own account puts him already turning that problem over here; the account was written thirty-nine years later.
suggested_refs: The Karolinum, historic seat of Charles-Ferdinand University, Prague
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla: Inventor of the Electrical Age (2013), via citation

stops.name: Budapest, the diagram drawn in the sand
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Tesla later dated the insight to February 1882, in My Inventions (1919), thirty-seven years after the fact; Wikipedia says only that he claimed it for 1882, and Carlson reads the sudden vision in the park as retrospective construction. No notebook from 1882 survives.
stops.campa: He has come to Budapest for Tivadar Puskás and the new telephone exchange, where he rises to chief electrician, and he is walking in the Városliget at sunset reciting Faust with a friend when, by his own account, the thing arrives whole: a field of magnetism made to rotate by alternating currents, with no commutator and nothing sliding against the rotor to spark. He draws it in the sand of the path with a stick. Everything he will be paid for and cheated of across the next thirty years is in that diagram, and the only witness is the friend.
stops.quote: The idea came like a flash of lightning and in an instant the truth was revealed.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions, Chapter III, Electrical Experimenter (1919), via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Városliget at Budapest, and Tesla's account of the rotating-field vision in My Inventions
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: Paris, the Continental Edison Company
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; no month reached. Coordinates corrected to the company's offices at 57 rue de Clichy; the pool's pin lay 2 km away near Châtelet.
stops.campa: Puskás sends him on to the Continental Edison Company in Paris, the European licensee, where he repairs and improves lighting plants and is sent out to the manufacturing works at Ivry-sur-Seine to find faults that other engineers cannot. He is paid well, spends it at billiards, and swims in the Seine before the office each morning. He describes the rotating field to the management and, he says, is not understood. Carlson finds no company record of any such offer. The episode rests on a memoir he wrote thirty-seven years afterward.
suggested_refs: The Continental Edison Company offices at 57 rue de Clichy, and the generating works at Ivry-sur-Seine
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: Strasbourg, the motor built in off-hours
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and for a working prototype built at Strasbourg; no month reached. The circumstances, the borrowed shop and the unpaid bonus, come from My Inventions and are his own telling.
stops.campa: The company sends him to Strasbourg, where the new railway station's Edison plant has short-circuited during a lighting ceremony before the German emperor's officials. He repairs it. In the off-hours, in a borrowed machine shop, he builds from memory the motor he sketched in the Budapest sand and runs it: a rotor turning with nothing touching it, driven by the field alone. The first man to see it work is a local mechanic. Promised a bonus in Paris for the Strasbourg repair, he goes back for it and is not paid.
suggested_refs: The Strasbourg railway station power plant, site of the first working induction motor

segments.name: The Atlantic and the Edison Works

stops.name: New York, landing at Castle Garden
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1884; no day reached. The port of departure is contested and no stop is pinned for it: the tradition names Le Havre, while the ship the same tradition names, the City of Richmond, worked the Inman Line's Liverpool and Queenstown run.
stops.campa: He lands at Castle Garden in the Battery with a letter from Charles Batchelor to Thomas Edison, a book of poems, calculations for a flying machine, and by his own count four cents. The crossing that brought him is half legend: the port is disputed and the stolen ticket is his own story. The letter is not disputed. Edison, thirty-seven years old and the most famous man in American industry, reads it that night and sends the new arrival straight down to the pier to put a steamer's dynamos right before morning.
suggested_refs: Castle Garden immigration depot at the Battery, landing point in June 1884
sources: John J. O'Neill, Prodigal Genius (1944), via citation

stops.name: New York, the Edison Machine Works on Goerck Street
stops.date_confidence: attested: about six months of employment from June 1884, resignation in December 1884 over the unpaid bonus. The size of the promised bonus and Edison's reply are Tesla's account and are disputed by Edison's biographers.
stops.campa: At the Edison Machine Works on Goerck Street he redesigns the direct-current dynamos, works eighteen-hour days, and is told, he says, that fifty thousand dollars waits on success. When he asks for it he is told the offer was American humor, and is offered a raise of ten dollars a week instead. Edison's biographers dispute the whole scene. Nothing disputes the diary, which carries for that December two words in a black-ruled box: Good By to the Edison Machine Works. Direct current and alternating current now have their men.
stops.quote: I have had many hard-working assistants but you take the cake.
stops.quote_source: Thomas Edison to Tesla at the Edison Machine Works, quoted in Nikola Tesla, My Inventions, Chapter IV, Electrical Experimenter (1919), via Wikisource
suggested_refs: Tesla's diary page for December 1884, 'Good By to the Edison Machine Works'

stops.name: Rahway, the company that keeps the patents
stops.date_confidence: the company's formation is attested to 1885 by the pool's chronology lens and the investors' walkout to 1886; the pool's geography lens dated the venture 1886 to 1887 instead. The 1885 formation is used and the disagreement recorded. No month reached.
stops.campa: Lemuel Serrell, a patent attorney, brings him Robert Lane and Benjamin Vail, and Tesla Electric Light and Manufacturing is formed with a plant at Rahway. They want arc lamps for the streets of the town, not his motor. He gives them arc lamps and his first American patents, and in 1886 they take the patents, hand him a stock certificate, and walk away from the company. He is left with nothing he can eat. Through that winter he digs ditches in New York for about two dollars a day and calls it, later, the hardest year of his life.
suggested_refs: Tesla Electric Light and Manufacturing Company, Rahway, New Jersey, and Tesla's first US patents for arc lighting

stops.name: New York, the laboratory at 89 Liberty Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1887 for the formation of the Tesla Electric Company; no day reached. US patent 381,968 issued in May 1888 and is carried in this campa.
stops.campa: Alfred Brown of Western Union and the lawyer Charles Peck listen to a ditch-digger describe a motor with no commutator, and ask to be shown. He spins a copper egg upright on a table inside a rotating field, and they open a laboratory for him at 89 Liberty Street. In under a year the whole polyphase system is drawn, built, and filed: generator, transmission line, motor, all of it alternating, all of it his. Patent 381,968 issues in May 1888. He is thirty-one and has been in the country four years.
stops.quote: In our dynamo machines, it is well known, we generate alternate currents which we direct by means of a commutator, a complicated device.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, 'A New System of Alternate Current Motors and Transformers,' AIEE lecture 1888, in T. C. Martin, ed., The Inventions, Researches and Writings of Nikola Tesla (1894)
suggested_refs: US Patent 381,968, 'Electro-Magnetic Motor,' granted May 1888
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: New York, the lecture to the electrical engineers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates corrected by 5.5 km: Columbia College stood at Madison Avenue and 49th Street in 1888 and did not move to Morningside Heights until 1897; the pool had pinned the City Hall district.
stops.campa: Before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, in Columbia College's rooms at Madison Avenue and Forty-ninth Street, he reads the paper that ends the argument about alternating current: a new system of motors and transformers, working machines to hand, mathematics any man in the room can check. William Anthony has already run the motors at Cornell and found them the equal of the best direct-current machines. George Westinghouse, in Pittsburgh, reads the account of the evening and sends for the patents within weeks.
stops.quote: The subject which I now have the pleasure of bringing to your notice is a novel system of electric distribution and transmission of power by means of alternate currents.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, 'A New System of Alternate Current Motors and Transformers,' lecture to the AIEE, 16 May 1888, in T. C. Martin, ed. (1894), Project Gutenberg ebook 39272
suggested_refs: The AIEE lecture of 16 May 1888, printed in Martin's Inventions, Researches and Writings (1894)
sources: T. C. Martin, ed., The Inventions, Researches and Writings of Nikola Tesla (1894)

stops.name: New York, the Westinghouse contract
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1888 for the terms; no day reached. Place corrected: the pool located the deal at Pittsburgh, but Westinghouse came to Tesla's Manhattan laboratory and Tesla moved to Pittsburgh only afterward, as consultant.
stops.campa: Westinghouse comes to the Liberty Street laboratory himself and buys: five thousand dollars in cash and one hundred and fifty shares of company stock, the package commonly reckoned at sixty thousand, plus two dollars and fifty cents of royalty on every horsepower of alternating current the company ever sells, plus two thousand a month to come to Pittsburgh as consultant. It is the largest sum anyone will ever pay him. The royalty clause, left alone, would have paid him on every horsepower sold for the life of the patents. O'Neill's biography turns that into the richest man in America.
suggested_refs: The Westinghouse licensing agreement of July 1888, with its per-horsepower royalty clause

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the year at the Westinghouse works
stops.date_confidence: inferred. About a year at the works is attested, running from late 1888 into 1889; no month is given in the sources and November is a placeholder inside the attested span.
stops.campa: He spends about a year at the Westinghouse works trying to make his motor fit a company that has already standardized on 133 cycles for its lighting. His motors want sixty. The engineers have their apparatus and their contracts; he has a system designed whole and no wish to see it cut into pieces. In the end the company will build to sixty cycles, the figure that runs North America to this day, and he goes back to New York in 1889. He does not take a post in another man's works again.
suggested_refs: The frequency dispute at the Westinghouse works, settled at sixty cycles
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the royalty released
stops.date_confidence: the year 1891 and the release of the per-horsepower royalty are attested; no month reached. The scene in which Tesla tears up the contract is O'Neill (1944) and is tradition. Place strain flagged: the pool put the episode at Pittsburgh, but Tesla had returned to New York in 1889; the pin is the company's works, not his address.
stops.campa: Westinghouse Electric, overextended by the current war and by Wall Street, is told by its bankers to shed the Tesla royalty or be broken up, and Westinghouse comes and says so. Tesla releases the clause. The scene in which he tears the contract to pieces in front of the man comes from O'Neill's biography of 1944, written by a friend when both were dead; the instrument was a renegotiated agreement. What is not in dispute is that he gave up the money, kept his patents in the field, and never asked for it back.
suggested_refs: The renegotiated Westinghouse agreement of 1891, surrendering the per-horsepower royalty
sources: John J. O'Neill, Prodigal Genius (1944), via citation

stops.name: New York, the coil and the citizenship
stops.date_confidence: the naturalization is attested to 30 July 1891. The Tesla coil is dated to 1891 with US patent 454,622 granted the same year; the pool had it built in summer 1889 and patented the following year, which neither date supports. Laboratory address corrected: 175 Grand Street runs 1889 to 1892, not 1892 to 1895.
stops.campa: At the Grand Street laboratory he builds the air-core resonant transformer that will carry his name and patents it the same year, and with it opens the high-frequency work: lamps burning with no wire running to them, currents drawn over his own skin to show that they do not burn. On the thirtieth of July he takes the oath as a citizen of the United States. His friends say afterward that he kept the naturalization papers in his safe and left the medals loose in a drawer. He is thirty-five and famous on two continents.
suggested_refs: US Patent 454,622, 'System of Electric Lighting,' 1891, and the 175 Grand Street laboratory
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: London, the evening at the Royal Institution
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: He gives the Royal Institution in Albemarle Street an evening of high-potential currents: tubes glowing in his bare hand, a lamp lit across the room with nothing between, a field filling the theatre. The Institution asks him to stay and repeat it for the electrical engineers, and he does. Faraday's own room is opened to him and he is shown the chair. The lectures are printed and reprinted, and the reputation he leaves in London is what Belgrade will receive him with three months later.
suggested_refs: Tesla's 1892 Royal Institution lecture on experiments with alternate currents of high potential and high frequency
sources: T. C. Martin, ed., The Inventions, Researches and Writings of Nikola Tesla (1894)

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne and the telegram
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1892 for the lecture; no day reached. The telegram scene is Tesla's own account in My Inventions.
stops.campa: He repeats the lecture in Paris for the Société Internationale des Électriciens and is fêted through a week of dinners he would rather not attend. A telegram reaches him there: his mother is dying at Gospić. He leaves the tour where it stands and takes the trains east. He has been in America eight years and has not gone back once, and he is going home for the first time as the most celebrated electrician in Europe, to a house in the Lika where his mother built the looms with her own hands.
suggested_refs: The Paris high-frequency lecture of February 1892 before the Société Internationale des Électriciens

stops.name: Gospić, the vigil and the vision
stops.date_confidence: the year of Đuka Mandić's death rests on the Tesla Universe timeline alone; the month of April comes from the pool's geography lens and no primary record was reached. The vision is Tesla's own account.
stops.campa: He reaches Đuka's bedside before the end and sits the vigil with his sisters. She dies, and he collapses and is put to bed in another room of the same house, and there, he writes afterward, he sees a cloud carrying angelic figures, one of them his mother, and hears music. He then explains the vision to himself in print as a remembered painting and the strain of grief. It is the only passage in his autobiography where he argues with himself in public, and he leaves both halves of the argument standing.
suggested_refs: The account of Đuka Mandić's death and the vision, My Inventions, Chapter II

stops.name: Belgrade, received as a national possession
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The date and the reception rest on contemporary Belgrade press accounts cited in Carlson; no press text was read in this pass.
stops.campa: On the way back he stops in Belgrade, and a Serbian kingdom that has never had a famous man of science receives one. Crowds meet the train; King Alexander decorates him; the Royal Academy reads him a formal address. He is the subject of no Serbian king, having been born under the Austrian emperor and naturalized in New York the year before, and Belgrade claims him entire regardless. Sixty-five years from this afternoon his ashes will come to this city, and a museum will be built to hold them.
suggested_refs: The Serbian Royal Academy address to Tesla, Belgrade, 1892
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), citing Belgrade press accounts, via citation

segments.name: The White City and the Falls

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Franklin Institute lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates corrected by 1.2 km: in 1893 the Franklin Institute occupied its hall at 15 South 7th Street, and the Benjamin Franklin Parkway building the pool pinned did not open until 1934.
stops.campa: At the Institute's hall on South Seventh Street, four decades before the marble building on the Parkway exists, he lectures on light and other high-frequency phenomena and puts the apparatus of wireless transmission in front of a room of engineers: a transmitter, a tuned receiver, and no wire between them. He repeats the demonstration at St Louis in March for the electric light men. The apparatus is what his lawyers will set against Marconi's priority in the courts for the next fifty years, and Tesla at this date is chiefly interested in lighting.
suggested_refs: Tesla's 1893 lecture 'On Light and Other High Frequency Phenomena,' Franklin Institute, 15 South 7th Street
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: Chicago, the White City lit by his system
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Exposition season, May to October 1893; the day is the fair's opening. Pin inherited byte-identical from the corpus Columbian Exposition coordinate carried in muybridge.journey.json.
stops.campa: Westinghouse underbids General Electric and lights the World's Columbian Exposition with Tesla's polyphase system: a quarter of a million lamps, a plain of white plaster burning after dark, and the fair is called the White City for it. Tesla walks the ground and runs high-frequency current through his own body to light lamps in his hands. On the same grounds Muybridge is showing moving pictures in the Zoopraxographical Hall, Vivekananda addresses the Parliament of Religions in September, and Sitting Bull's cabin is reassembled for paying visitors.
suggested_refs: The Westinghouse polyphase installation at the World's Columbian Exposition, Jackson Park and the Midway Plaisance
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: New York, the South Fifth Avenue fire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Address corrected: the fire took the fourth-floor laboratory at 33-35 South Fifth Avenue, occupied 1892 to 1895; the pool had swapped this with 175 Grand Street and attached the fire to the wrong building.
stops.campa: On the fourth floor of 33-35 South Fifth Avenue, in the small hours, fire takes the laboratory and everything standing in it: the mechanical oscillators, the wireless apparatus, the notes of four years, the models promised to Niagara. The building is gutted from the roof down and nothing is insured. He walks the street the next morning and cannot answer the reporters. Within the year he has rebuilt the whole program from memory at 46 East Houston Street, and what was on paper before that morning is known only from what he could still remember of it.
suggested_refs: The New York Times report of 14 March 1895 on the burning of Tesla's laboratory
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: Niagara Falls, the Adams station starts
stops.date_confidence: attested for transmission running from August 1895 to November 1896; no day reached. Pin inherited byte-identical from the corpus Niagara coordinate carried in jules_verne.journey.json; the Adams station's own position is 43.0896, -79.0378, recorded in the report.
stops.campa: The Adams station on the Niagara gorge starts its Westinghouse generators, built to his patents, and the current runs twenty-six miles to Buffalo: the first great long-distance transmission, and the end of the argument. Lord Kelvin, who chaired the international commission that chose polyphase alternating current over direct, had come to these falls opposed to it. Jules Verne stood at this same water in 1867 and put it in a novel. The family story has Tesla telling his uncles at seventeen that he would take the power out of Niagara.
suggested_refs: The Adams Power Station at Niagara Falls, first large-scale AC transmission, 1895 to 1896
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: New York, the teleautomaton in Madison Square Garden
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1898 for the electrical exhibition and the demonstration; no month or day reached, September is a placeholder. The pin is a reconstruction: no reachable source gave a coordinate, so the second Madison Square Garden's known position at Madison Square is used.
stops.campa: At the electrical exhibition in Madison Square Garden he floats a small iron boat in a tank and steers it by wireless from the rail, starting it, turning it, dousing and lighting its lamps while the crowd hunts for the wire. He calls it a teleautomaton. He offers it to the United States Navy as a guided torpedo and is refused. The patent issues as number 613,809, covering the control of a vessel by wireless. Nothing is manufactured from it in his lifetime, and the crowd goes on hunting for the wire.
stops.quote: My theory has always been that military men are superior to civilians in courtesy.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, letter to the editor, The New York Times, 2 May 1907, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: US Patent 613,809, the radio-controlled boat, and the 1898 Madison Square Garden electrical exhibition

stops.name: Colorado Springs, the station on Knob Hill
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1899 to early January 1900, the final journal entry being 7 January 1900; no day reached for the arrival. Coordinates corrected by 3.4 km: the station stood on Knob Hill at East Kiowa Street and North Foote Avenue, east of town, not in the foothills west of it. Razed 1904.
stops.campa: On Knob Hill, east of town where the air is thin and dry storms walk the plain, he raises a barn with a mast through its roof and a coil fifty feet across, and makes lightning: discharges of a hundred and thirty-five feet, thunder heard fifteen miles out, the El Paso Electric station burned out by what he draws from it. He measures standing waves in the earth itself and concludes that the planet can be used as a conductor. In December his receiver returns a repeating signal, and he will publish that it may have come from Mars.
stops.quote: The modulations of the human voice can be reproduced more clearly through the earth than through wire.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, quoted in 'Nikola Tesla Sees a Wireless Vision,' The New York Times, 3 October 1915, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: Tesla's Colorado Springs Notes, 1899-1900, and the Collier's Weekly article 'Talking With Planets,' 9 February 1901

stops.name: Shoreham, the tower begun at Wardenclyffe
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1901 for the Morgan agreement, with construction beginning in September 1901; no day reached. Coordinates from the pool's afterlife lens, which matches the published Wardenclyffe position; the geography lens pinned the site 1.4 km away.
stops.campa: J. P. Morgan gives him a hundred and fifty thousand dollars for fifty-one percent of the wireless patents, and Stanford White draws the tower: 187 feet of latticed timber on Long Island potato ground, an iron dome above it and shafts driven deep into the earth beneath, because the earth is half of the machine. He tells Morgan the thing is for wireless telegraphy. What he intends is power, broadcast to any point on the globe with no meter on it, and he does not put that in a letter until the money is spent.
suggested_refs: Wardenclyffe Tower at Shoreham, Long Island, designed with Stanford White, begun September 1901

stops.name: Shoreham, the money stops
stops.date_confidence: contradiction printed, not resolved: Wikipedia's Tesla article gives 1905 for the halt, while its Wardenclyffe Tower article says work effectively ceased around 1906 when Morgan refused further funding. Best reading is that staff were let go and work slowed in 1905 and the project was abandoned in 1906. No month reached.
stops.campa: Marconi has already sent the letter S across the Atlantic in December 1901 with cheap apparatus and no tower, and the money that would have finished Wardenclyffe goes to him instead. Morgan refuses more. The staff go in 1905 and the last of the work stops in 1906, the two standard accounts of the date differing by a year. The press begins printing the word hoax. He keeps the deed, mortgages it to the Waldorf-Astoria against his bill, and goes on writing to the newspapers about who invented what.
stops.quote: If I were not prompted to do so by a sense of fairness and pride I would be by the power I have of inventing anything I please.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, letter to the editor, The New York Times, 2 May 1907, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: Morgan's refusal of further funding for Wardenclyffe, and Tesla's newspaper letters on wireless priority

stops.name: New York, the suites at the Waldorf-Astoria
stops.date_confidence: the Waldorf residence runs through the 1900s to 1918, when Tesla left owing roughly twenty thousand dollars; the pool compressed the whole hotel sequence to 1918, which swallows four decades. No start date is attested and 1900 is a placeholder inside the attested span.
stops.campa: He keeps rooms at the Waldorf-Astoria on Fifth Avenue for years and receives there as a man of means; Mark Twain is among the friends who come, and a fixture at the laboratory besides. The bill runs on unpaid until 1918, when he leaves owing about twenty thousand dollars and the hotel holds his baggage against the debt, apparatus and models among it, never recovered. From here he moves whenever the credit runs out, through the St Regis, the Hotel Marguery, the Governor Clinton and the Hotel Pennsylvania, one address at a time.
suggested_refs: The Waldorf-Astoria on Fifth Avenue, Tesla's address through the Wardenclyffe years
sources: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla (2013), via citation

stops.name: New York, the Edison Medal
stops.date_confidence: the award year is 1916 per the IEEE recipient list and Wikipedia's infobox; 18 May 1917 is the presentation banquet, which teslasociety.com reports as the award date. The stop is dated to the banquet. The pin is a reconstruction of the engineering societies' building address; no coordinate was sourced.
stops.campa: The American Institute of Electrical Engineers votes him the Edison Medal for 1916 and holds the banquet in May 1917, and he nearly does not come to it. The story his friends tell is that he was found feeding pigeons in the park and walked back to the hall in time to be presented. He accepts a medal bearing the face of the man who told him a promised bonus was American humor, and the room applauds the system that beat that man's system, at a dinner given in his own honor.
suggested_refs: The AIEE Edison Medal, awarded 1916, presented at a banquet on 18 May 1917

stops.name: Shoreham, the tower dynamited
stops.date_confidence: attested for a demolition running July to September 1917 by the Smiley Steel Company of New York, with salvage of 1,750 dollars. The specific date of 4 July given in the pool is unsupported and the day is dropped; July here is the start of the attested window.
stops.campa: The Smiley Steel Company of New York, working for the creditors, sets charges in the tower's legs and brings the thing down in stages across the summer. The salvage sells for seventeen hundred and fifty dollars against a debt many times that. The tower had never transmitted anything. He is in Manhattan while it comes down, and no account places him at Shoreham that summer. The laboratory building Stanford White drew is left standing on the site, and stands there yet.
stops.quote: Wireless is coming to mankind in its full meaning like a hurricane some of these days.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, quoted in 'Nikola Tesla Sees a Wireless Vision,' The New York Times, 3 October 1915, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The demolition of Wardenclyffe Tower, July to September 1917, for 1,750 dollars in scrap

stops.name: New York, My Inventions in six parts
stops.date_confidence: attested: six parts in Electrical Experimenter, February through June and October 1919, introduced by Hugo Gernsback; first issued as a standalone book in 1982. The pin is the Hotel St Regis, one address in the attested hotel sequence of these years, not a documented place of writing.
stops.campa: He writes his life for Hugo Gernsback's Electrical Experimenter, six parts from February to October, in a magazine that prints scientific romances beside them. It is the fullest account there will ever be of the childhood, the Budapest park and the Edison year, and it is written between thirty and sixty years after the events by a man in a hotel room with no notebooks left, most of them having burned in 1895. Most of the standard biography descends from these pages. No publisher makes a book of it until 1982.
stops.quote: I do not rush into actual work. When I get an idea I start at once building it up in my imagination.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions, Chapter I, Electrical Experimenter (1919), via Wikisource
suggested_refs: My Inventions, serialized in Electrical Experimenter, February to October 1919

stops.name: New York, the cover of Time at seventy-five
stops.date_confidence: attested to the cover date of 20 July 1931. Age corrected: Tesla turned 75 in July 1931, not 81; the pool transposed his age at the 1937 taxicab accident onto this event. Coordinates corrected: the Hotel Pennsylvania stood at 401 Seventh Avenue, and the pool had duplicated the Hotel New Yorker's pin for it.
stops.campa: Time puts him on the cover for his seventy-fifth birthday, in profile against a coil discharge, captioned All the world's his power house, and letters come from scientists across Europe with Einstein among them. He is at the Hotel Pennsylvania on Seventh Avenue in these years, moving hotel by hotel as the credit runs out, and he spends his mornings in the parks feeding pigeons and carrying the injured ones up to his room. The inventions he announces to reporters now are announced without apparatus to show.
suggested_refs: Time magazine cover, 20 July 1931, 'All the world's his power house'

stops.name: New York, the Hotel New Yorker and the teleforce
stops.date_confidence: attested: the move to the Hotel New Yorker is dated 1934, and the teleforce announcement to his 78th birthday, reported 11 July 1934. Coordinates corrected to 481 Eighth Avenue; the pool had given this building the Hotel Pennsylvania's pin.
stops.campa: He takes rooms on the thirty-third floor of the Hotel New Yorker on Eighth Avenue, where he will live out the last nine years, and on his seventy-eighth birthday he gives the reporters teleforce: a beam of particles thrown through open air that would drop ten thousand aircraft at two hundred miles and make any country's borders impassable. He describes four inventions in combination and declines to describe the apparatus. There is no apparatus. The papers call it a death ray, which he dislikes, and print it anyway.
stops.quote: These four inventions in combination enable man to loose in free air forces beyond conception.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, quoted in 'Beam to Kill Army at 200 Miles, Tesla's Claim on 78th Birthday,' New York Herald Tribune, 11 July 1934, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The teleforce particle-beam announcement of 11 July 1934, and Tesla's rooms at the Hotel New Yorker
sources: New York Herald Tribune, 11 July 1934, via Wikisource

stops.name: New York, death in Room 3327
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, with time of death estimated at 10:30 p.m. and cause given as coronary thrombosis. Discovery interval corrected: both lenses of the research pool said the body lay two days undiscovered; Wikipedia says the maid found him the next day, and it was the Do Not Disturb sign that had hung three days.
stops.campa: In the autumn of 1937, eighty-one years old, he is knocked down by a taxicab crossing a street on his way to feed the pigeons, and refuses to see a doctor. He does not recover from it. On the night of the seventh of January 1943 he dies alone in Room 3327, coronary thrombosis, at about half past ten. The Do Not Disturb sign has hung on the door three days; the maid finds him the next morning, which several accounts turn into two days undiscovered. He is eighty-six and owes the hotel money.
suggested_refs: Room 3327 of the Hotel New Yorker, 481 Eighth Avenue

stops.name: New York, the Office of Alien Property takes the room
stops.date_confidence: attested: the FBI asked the Office of Alien Property Custodian to seize the belongings two days after the death. The pool tagged this as tradition and gave the wrong legal basis; the hook was the foreign citizenship of the claimant, Sava Kosanović, not Tesla's own status.
stops.campa: Two days after the death the Federal Bureau of Investigation asks the Office of Alien Property Custodian to take everything in the room and the safe, because the claimant, his nephew Sava Kosanović, is not an American citizen. Tesla had been one since 1891. John G. Trump of MIT reads the impounded papers and reports no weapon in them and no death ray. The wireless priority he argued for forty years is settled partly in his favor by the Supreme Court in June, five months after his death. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman will one day share a prize named for Marconi.
stops.quote: A wireless telephone conversation can be made as secret as thought.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, quoted in 'Nikola Tesla Sees a Wireless Vision,' The New York Times, 3 October 1915, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Office of Alien Property Custodian seizure of January 1943 and John G. Trump's report

stops.name: New York, the funeral at St John the Divine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the cathedral service and the cremation at Ferncliff. La Guardia's eulogy was read on 10 January, two days earlier. The three Nobel laureates said to have served as pallbearers could not be confirmed against a primary source and are tradition.
stops.campa: Two thousand come to the Cathedral of St John the Divine, which is Episcopal, for a Serbian Orthodox service over a Serb of the Austrian Empire who died an American. Roosevelt sends condolences and so does King Peter II of Yugoslavia from exile; La Guardia's eulogy had gone out on the radio two days before. Three Nobel laureates are said to have carried him, a detail repeated everywhere and confirmed nowhere. The body goes to Ferncliff at Hartsdale the same day and is burned.
suggested_refs: The Cathedral of St John the Divine, and Ferncliff Cemetery crematory at Hartsdale

stops.name: Belgrade, the museum at Krunska 51
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the founding decision. The pool collapsed three dates into one 1957: the effects were shipped from New York on 7 September 1951, the permanent exhibition opened in 1955, and the urn went on public display in 1957. Coordinates corrected to Krunska 51; the geography lens pinned 500 m away.
stops.campa: Kosanović ships his uncle's papers and effects out of New York on the seventh of September 1951, and the government of the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia establishes the Nikola Tesla Museum by decision of the fifth of December 1952, in a villa built in 1927 for Đorđe Genčić at Krunska 51. The permanent exhibition opens in 1955; the urn goes on public display in 1957, on a marble pedestal, and the house becomes his tomb. In 2003 the archive enters UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
suggested_refs: The Nikola Tesla Museum, Krunska 51, Belgrade, and the urn holding his ashes

stops.name: Paris, the unit is given his name
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1960 for the General Conference on Weights and Measures decision, on the proposal of France Avčin; no month reached. The pin is a reconstruction: the conference city is given as Paris in the sources and no session coordinate was sought.
stops.campa: The General Conference on Weights and Measures, at the proposal of the Slovenian engineer France Avčin, gives the SI unit of magnetic flux density his name. One tesla is one weber per square metre. The man who died owing a hotel bill becomes a quantity: every magnetic resonance scanner built afterward is rated in teslas, and the figure is printed on the housing where the patient can read it. He has been seventeen years dead, and out of fashion in America for longer than that.
suggested_refs: The 1960 General Conference on Weights and Measures and the SI unit of magnetic flux density

stops.name: Smiljan, the house rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the Nikola Tesla Memorial Center opened on 10 July 2006, the 150th anniversary of the birth.
stops.campa: On the hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the midnight birth, the reconstructed house at Smiljan opens as the Nikola Tesla Memorial Center: the priest's house raised again, the Church of St Peter and Paul beside it where his father served, a statue by Mile Blažević, and working models in a barn where a field can be watched turning. The village had been burned in the war of the 1990s and the house went with it, so what stands on these coordinates is built new, on the old footings, in time for the anniversary.

stops.name: Shoreham, the site bought back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the purchase; the crowdfunding campaign ran from August 2012 and Musk's pledge came in July 2014.
stops.campa: The cartoonist Matthew Inman puts the derelict Wardenclyffe site to the internet in August 2012 and raises one million three hundred and seventy thousand dollars inside a week, most of it from people who learned about Tesla online. The Tesla Science Center completes the purchase on the second of May 2013. In July 2014 Elon Musk, whose car company took the name in 2003 from founders who chose it before he joined them, adds a million dollars and a charging station. The tower's foundation is still under the grass.

stops.name: Belgrade, the petition to the Holy Synod
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Month corrected: the pool gave 7 July, transposing the date; the petition was submitted on 7 January 2021, which is both the anniversary of the death and Orthodox Christmas.
stops.campa: On the seventh of January 2021, the anniversary of the death and the Orthodox Christmas together, the Tesla Science Foundation Serbia submits to the Holy Synod of the Serbian Orthodox Church a petition to consider the canonization of Nikola Tesla, proposing the tenth of July for his feast day. The Synod has not ruled. The priest's son who would not go to the seminary, who took his father's promise at a sickbed in Smiljan and spent it on engineering, is put to his father's church as a saint.
